findings.headline: Housing land supply has fallen to 4.9 years, below the 5-year statutory requirement
findings.detail: Following the King's Newton Lane appeal decision, the council's five-year housing land supply has reduced to 4.9 years, falling below the statutory 5-year housing land supply requirement. The council is implementing mitigation measures including review of strategic allocations in Part 1 of the Local Plan, with completion required by 31 December 2026.
findings.matters: A housing land supply below the 5-year requirement makes the council more vulnerable to planning appeals and can constrain development revenue and housing growth targets. It also indicates planning policy vulnerabilities that lenders monitor as indicators of local governance effectiveness.
findings.figures: 4.9 years (below 5-year requirement); Local Plan deadline 31 December 2026
findings.quote: the Council's five-year housing land supply has reduced to 4.9 years. Mitigating actions are in place to address this position ahead of the Local Plan deadline of 31 December 2026.

findings.headline: Depot operations business case withdrawn due to financial constraints
findings.detail: The council's project to review depot operations and secure alternative accommodation has been withdrawn due to financial constraints. The business case was originally scheduled for presentation to Finance & Management Committee in January 2026 and Council in February 2026 but has been deferred, with alternative options now to be presented in June 2026.
findings.matters: Deferral of capital maintenance projects due to financial constraints indicates the council is prioritizing immediate spending over essential asset maintenance, which raises concerns about asset condition and long-term capital liabilities.
findings.figures: Business case deferred from January/February 2026 to June 2026
findings.quote: this has been withdrawn due to the financial constraints faced by the Council. Alternative options will be presented to Environmental and Development Services Committee in June 2026.

findings.headline: Strategic financial risk rating escalated to 12 due to geopolitical impacts on fuel and utilities spending
findings.detail: The council's overall mitigated risk rating for decreasing financial resources has increased from 9 to 12 to reflect geopolitical landscape risks impacting council operations indirectly through spending on fuel and utilities. While the council has balanced its 2026/27 budget, the escalation reflects growing concerns about cost pressures via council and third-party contractor spending.
findings.matters: Escalating financial risk ratings indicate the council is facing tightening financial conditions, which directly impacts its ability to service borrowing and maintain service delivery. Lenders need to understand the trajectory of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased from 9 to 12
findings.quote: The overall mitigated risk rating has increased from 9 to 12 to reflect the geopolitical landscape during Quarter 4, 2025/26, and the potential this has to impact Council operations indirectly through spend on fuel and utilities via Council and third party contractor spend.

findings.headline: 2027/28 is final sovereign budget year before April 2028 reorganisation, creating dual pressures on budget decisions
findings.detail: The council must balance immediate service needs against creating a sustainable financial legacy for the new unitary authority. The document acknowledges this 'dual responsibility' and states budget decisions 'will influence not only current service delivery, but also the resilience, flexibility and sustainability of the future Unitary Council.'
findings.matters: Reorganisation-driven budget pressures could force decisions that create structural problems or hidden liabilities for the successor authority, affecting its creditworthiness and creating unexpected costs for existing and future lenders to the unitary council.
findings.figures: April 2028 reorganisation vesting date; 2027/28 is final standalone budget year
findings.quote: 2027/28 is the final year of sovereign budget setting ahead of local government reorganisation. Every decision carries a dual responsibility, therefore the Council has to balance meeting the needs of our residents, while maintaining a sustainable financial position. The decisions made will influence not only current service delivery, but also the resilience, flexibility and sustainability of the future Unitary Council.

findings.headline: Post-2028/29 funding is highly uncertain, affecting forecast reliability for 2029/30 and 2030/31
findings.detail: The 3-year funding settlement ends 2028/29. Beyond that, funding depends on yet-to-be-determined Fair Funding Review reforms, business rates baseline reset, council tax policy changes, and grant redistribution. This makes 2029/30 and 2030/31 forecasts speculative, representing 40% of the council's medium-term financial projections.
findings.matters: Lenders assess creditworthiness on forward forecasts. Uncertainty covering half the forecast period undermines the reliability of the council's financial plan and its ability to demonstrate sustainable repayment capacity beyond the settlement period.
findings.figures: Uncertainty applies to 2029/30 and 2030/31 (2 of 5 forecast years); combined deficits in uncertain years: £10,545,623
findings.quote: Beyond the three-year Local Government Finance Settlement period to 2028/29, there remains a significant degree of uncertainty over the level and distribution of local government funding. Whilst the multi-year settlement provides greater short to medium-term planning certainty, future years will continue to be influenced by the implementation of the Fair Funding Review reforms, the reset of the business rates retention system, council tax referendum limits and the consolidation or redistribution of existing grants.

findings.headline: Service expenditure overrunning by £226,500 in 2026/27 despite £1.65m in cost-saving initiatives
findings.detail: The 2026/27 forecast shows the council running £226,500 worse than budget due to service expenditure overspends, partially offset by additional planning income. This occurs despite the Budget Optimisation Board delivering £1.65m in savings across service reviews (£351k), vacancies (£253k), commercial income (£258k), and new opportunities (£795k), suggesting underlying cost control difficulties.
findings.matters: It indicates the council struggles to control operational spending even after implemented savings, raising concerns about deliverability of future Sustainable Finance Programme targets needed to address multi-year budget gaps.
findings.figures: £227,134 actual deficit vs £634 budgeted; £226,500 unfavourable variance; £1,655,766 delivered savings across four categories
findings.quote: The current forecast position on the General fund for 2026/27 is a deficit for the year of £227,134 compared to a budgeted deficit of £634. This is an overall increase on budgeted deficit of £226,500. The main variations to budget are overspends in service expenditure, being offset by additional planning income.

findings.headline: Regulatory cost pressures from Awaabs law and new legislation adding £21k+ to HRA repairs
findings.detail: HRA responsive repairs show £109k adverse variance 'in part due to new legislation'. Specifically, compensation payments increased £21k 'due to increases following Awaabs law'. Council notes fire contractor appointment for passive fire protection works with £400k earmarked reserve embedded in budget.
findings.matters: Unfunded legislative requirements imposing costs on housing authority. Awaabs law response suggests trend of increasing regulatory burden on social housing.
findings.figures: £21k compensation pressure from Awaabs law; £109k R&M adverse from new legislation
findings.quote: Compensation Payments - £21k adverse due to increases following Awaabs law.

findings.headline: Vehicle hire costs elevated due to fleet reliability issues in new refuse vehicles
findings.detail: £155k overspend in waste collection due to vehicle hire. Transport shows additional £122k variance including £69k diesel price pressure. Document states 'Vehicle hire costs remain above budget due to vehicle reliability issues and capacity shortfalls. Temporary vehicles have been hired to maintain service delivery while service issues with new refuse vehicles are addressed.' Spare parts costs also increased £30k 'due to damaged hire vehicle returns'.
findings.matters: Asset management issue: recently-purchased new fleet having reliability problems, forcing expensive temporary hire. Fleet replacement plan under review but no resolution timeline.
findings.figures: £155k van and RCV hire in waste; £69k HVO diesel pressure; £30k spare parts; £122k transport variance
findings.quote: Vehicle hire costs remain above budget due to vehicle reliability issues and capacity shortfalls. Temporary vehicles have been hired to maintain service delivery while service issues with new refuse vehicles are addressed.

findings.headline: Business rates funding cannot be forecast; contaminated data from appeals backlog
findings.detail: Council states explicitly: 'A business rates forecast has not been included in this report as system updates are required before the relevant information can be accurately produced.' Additionally, 'there is a significant increase in appeals due to the deadline for the 2023 listing. Therefore, the data is contaminated data due to speculation.' Position will be reviewed when system updates complete.
findings.matters: Retained business rates is a major funding stream (£3.446m budgeted). Unable to forecast in Q1 indicates either technical issue or appeals environment too volatile. Lenders need visibility of council's funding base.
findings.figures: £3.446m retained business rates budgeted; cannot be forecast
findings.quote: Furthermore, there is a significant increase in appeals due to the deadline for the 2023 listing. Therefore, the data is contaminated data due to speculation.

findings.headline: HGV driver recruitment failing: only 2 suitable candidates from 10 vacancies
findings.detail: Waste and transport services facing critical staffing gaps. 'Driver shortages resulted in missed collection rounds that required weekend recovery work, increasing overtime costs. Recent recruitment activity saw only two suitable candidates identified from ten vacancies, requiring the posts to be re-advertised.' Despite a recent pay increase, recruitment remains challenging.
findings.matters: Service delivery impact (missed collections) plus cost pressure (overtime and hired vehicles). Signals structural labor market challenge that won't resolve quickly.
findings.figures: 2 from 10 candidates; missed collection rounds requiring weekend recovery
findings.quote: Recent recruitment activity saw only two suitable candidates identified from ten vacancies, requiring the posts to be re-advertised.

findings.headline: 21% of operational workforce absent, driving £206k agency costs in waste collection alone
findings.detail: Household waste collection shows £391k overspend. Of this, £206k is agency staffing costs due to sickness and vacancies. Document states 'Around 21% of the workforce is currently absent, creating staffing pressures that require agency cover to maintain essential services. Attendance is being actively managed in line with Council policy.'
findings.matters: Absence rate of one-fifth of workforce is unusually high and indicates underlying HR/wellness issue. Mitigation plan (Employee Assistance Scheme) is reactive to the problem, not preventive.
findings.figures: 21% absence rate; £206k agency costs in waste alone
findings.quote: Around 21% of the workforce is currently absent, creating staffing pressures that require agency cover to maintain essential services.

findings.headline: £178k recycling credits at risk if County Council withholds April-May payments
findings.detail: Garden waste disposal transferred to Derbyshire County from April 2026. Council's contract with Biffa extended to June to align with food waste collections. Previously received recycling credits. County has not yet confirmed whether it will pay credits for the April-May transition period. Document states explicitly: 'In the event these do not materialise, there will be an additional cost of £178k, which has not been factored into this outturn.'
findings.matters: Material unforecasted risk worth nearly 80% of current GF deficit; outcome depends on another authority's decision.
findings.figures: £178k unbudgeted cost if credits not paid
findings.quote: In the event these do not materialise, there will be an additional cost of £178k, which has not been factored into this outturn.

findings.headline: Employee pay award for general staff not yet agreed, creating unquantified cost pressure
findings.detail: Chief Officer pay was agreed at 3.3% in June. Council budgeted 3.2% for general employees across General Fund and HRA, but a decision on employees' pay award has not yet been agreed. Document explicitly notes 'there is a potential pressure in the year'.
findings.matters: Unresolved payroll cost could widen current deficits if award exceeds 3.2% assumption.
findings.figures: Chief Officers 3.3% vs 3.2% budgeted for employees
findings.quote: A decision has not yet been agreed for employees. The Council has built in 3.2% across its General Fund and HRA and so there is a potential pressure in the year.

findings.headline: HRA deficit increased by £236k to £447k total due to rental income shortfall
findings.detail: HRA was budgeted for £211k deficit. Q1 forecast is £447k deficit. Main driver is rental income £201,735 below forecast due to delayed property purchases and increased voids.
findings.matters: Housing revenue is supposed to be self-financing. Income shortfall creates wider deficit and depends on uncertain Q3 property purchase completions.
findings.figures: £236k increased deficit; £201,735 rental income adverse variance; forecast deficit £447k vs budget £211k
findings.quote: Income - Rental Income collection lower than budgeted due to reduction in assumed number of properties purchased or brought back into use along with increased voids.

findings.headline: General Fund deficit of £227k materializing from approved balanced budget
findings.detail: The February 2026 budget was balanced with zero deficit. Q1 forecast shows £227k increased deficit, representing a 1% increase in the council's net spend. The forecast outturn position is £20.75m against budget of £20.52m.
findings.matters: Early in-year deficit indicates structural pressure or unforecasted cost drivers, suggesting the balanced budget assumption was not robust.
findings.figures: £227k increased deficit; 1% increase in net spend; forecast £20.75m vs budget £20.52m
findings.quote: The forecast outturn position at Quarter 1 on the General Fund is an increased deficit of £227k.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 ANTI-FRAUD AND& CORRUPTION PLAN AND COUNTER-FRAUD PARTNERSHIP PERFORMANCE UPDATE
findings.headline: Counter-Fraud Partnership cost £52,681 in 2025-26 but recovered savings of £355,389, significantly exceeding annual running cost.
findings.detail: The partnership with Derby City Council delivered £355,389.02 total savings in 2025-26: £118,663.47 in recovered cash from customers and £236,725.55 in prevented losses. This was an increase of £40,006.91 on the previous year and substantially exceeds the partnership cost.
findings.matters: The partnership consistently delivers returns well above its cost, improving the council's financial position through fraud detection and recovery.
findings.figures: Partnership cost: £52,681; Total savings: £355,389.02 (cashable £118,663.47, value-for-money £236,725.55); Year-on-year increase: £40,006.91
findings.quote: In 2025-26 the Partnership cost the Council £52,681 and delivered total savings of £355,389.02. This in an increase of £40,006.91 compared to the previous year.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 ANTI-FRAUD AND& CORRUPTION PLAN AND COUNTER-FRAUD PARTNERSHIP PERFORMANCE UPDATE
findings.headline: Ongoing criminal case involving an agency worker engaged in undisclosed dual employment within Housing Service, with trial scheduled April 2027.
findings.detail: An agency worker engaged by South Derbyshire's Housing Service from 2021-24 was found to have simultaneously worked for another English local authority without disclosure ('career polygamy'). The other authority has pursued legal action against the individual and their fraudulent contract lasted approximately 6 months. South Derbyshire has provided information to support the prosecution and the council may be called as a witness at trial.
findings.matters: This reveals a control weakness: an unauthorised dual employment in Housing went undetected for three years, raising questions about the council's contractor and agency worker vetting processes and oversight capabilities.
findings.figures: Agency worker employed 2021-24; other council's fraudulent contract approximately 6 months; court date April 2027
findings.quote: The Council received formal notification from another English local authority concerning an agency worker who had been engaged within the Housing Service from 2021-24. The notification advised that the individual in question had been found to be engaged in "career polygamy" – simultaneously undertaking paid work for more than one employer without proper disclosure.

findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit rates governance framework at Reasonable Assurance, not High, with ongoing monitoring required
findings.detail: The council's governance framework operates with Reasonable Assurance per the 2025/26 Internal Audit opinion. This standard assurance level, plus the explicit note that a small number of areas require ongoing improvement and monitoring, indicates material weaknesses remain.
findings.matters: Reasonable (not High) assurance means identified control weaknesses exist and future audit findings are likely, which affects financial reporting reliability and audit risk.
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance level
findings.quote: Overall, the Council's governance framework continues to operate with Reasonable Assurance, as reflected in the Head of Internal Audit opinion for 2025/26, although a small number of areas require ongoing improvement and monitoring.

findings.headline: Only 11 of 18 prior-year governance improvements completed; 7 remain underway and 2 new issues identified
findings.detail: Of the 18 improvements identified in 2024/25, 11 are now complete but 7 remain underway into 2025/26. Two additional improvements were identified during 2025/26. Prior issues with asset disposals and procurement compliance for agency staff carried forward from 2024/25.
findings.matters: Slow remediation of governance gaps, plus new issues identified, suggests systemic control weaknesses that take time to resolve and may affect audit and financial reporting.
findings.figures: 11 complete of 18; 7 underway; 2 new
findings.quote: Of the 18 improvements identified in 2024/25, 11 are complete and 7 remain underway (see Table 1 in Appendix 1). Two further improvements have been identified during 2025/26

findings.headline: Procurement Contract Regulations non-compliance identified in 2025/26 for agency staffing and supplies within Operational Services
findings.detail: The council identified further instances of non-compliance with Procurement Contract Regulations during 2025/26, with specific issues in agency staffing procurement and procurement of supplies/services within Operational Services. A procurement transformation programme is underway to address these and improve compliance with statutory requirements and Contract Procedure Rules.
findings.matters: Procurement non-compliance indicates internal control weaknesses over spend and contract management, which affects financial control and may expose the council to legal or financial risk.
findings.figures: Multiple instances identified; specific numbers not given in main text
findings.quote: In addition, further instances of non -compliance with Procurement Contract Regulations were identified during 2025/26, including in relation to agency staffing and the procurement of key supplies and services within Operational Services.
